gap: No result ChatGPT got states the battery figures on one common scale, hours of GPS workout recording: Apple Watch SE 3 7 h (Apple), Fitbit Charge 6 about 8 h (OutdoorGearLab measured; Google publishes no GPS figure), Garmin Lily 2 Active 9 h (Garmin) and Garmin vívoactive 6 20 h (OutdoorGearLab measured, 21 h claimed). The headline figures (18 h, 7 days, 9 days, 11 days) suggest a 15x spread, but GPS recording time is within 2 h across the three smaller wearables.
standout_why: I could not read the three cited rivals (womenshealthmag.com, goodhousekeeping.com, wired.com) or wearablebeat.com: WebFetch was blocked or returned 403, and fetching from the shell was denied. So this score comes from ChatGPT's answer, which repeats only the makers' headline numbers ('up to 7 days', 'up to 11 days', 'Battery life is shorter than Garmin or Fitbit'), plus search summaries of wearablebeat that say only that GPS 'drains the battery rapidly', with no hours. If a cited rival lists per-model GPS hours, this drops to 1. A person should check the three cited pages before relying on 2.
decides: The finding confirms the vívoactive 6 for running and long workouts: it is the only candidate that records more than 10 h of GPS, and it measured 20 h. It also weakens the 'Apple battery is much shorter' line for workouts: SE 3 GPS recording (7 h) is close to the Lily 2 Active (9 h) and the Charge 6 (about 8 h measured). The real Apple penalty is daily charging (18 h, with a 60-minute workout counted). The Lily 2 Active stays the small-wrist pick, and its 9 GPS hours cover anything up to a marathon. Footnote for the table: the vívoactive 6's 11 days becomes 5 days with the always-on display on (Garmin's spec, matched by OutdoorGearLab).
